title: Red Shift and the Expanding Universe

content.text: Red Shift and the Expanding Universe

In the 1920s, Edwin Hubble made one of the most profound discoveries in the history of science: the universe is expanding. He found that distant galaxies are moving away from us, and the farther away they are, the faster they're receding. This discovery revolutionised our understanding of the cosmos and provided crucial evidence for the Big Bang theory.

Red shift occurs when light from a source moving away is stretched to longer wavelengths. The greater the red shift of a galaxy, the faster it is receding and the further away it is. This relationship is described by Hubble's law: v = H0 x d.

— The galaxies themselves aren't moving much. Space itself is expanding, carrying galaxies with it.
— The universe includes all of space. It's not expanding into pre-existing space—space itself is stretching.
"There's a centre where the Big Bang happened"
— The Big Bang happened everywhere. Every point in space was at the origin.
"Red shift means objects are literally turning red"
— Red shift means the wavelength of light has increased. The object itself doesn't change colour.
"If the universe is expanding, so are we"
— Local structures (galaxies, solar systems, atoms) are held together by forces much stronger than the expansion.

Students often think galaxies are moving through space like rockets. In reality, space itself is expanding and carrying galaxies with it. The galaxies are not flying apart -- the fabric of space between them is stretching.

Red shift means the source is moving away (longer wavelength, lower frequency). Blue shift means the source is moving towards you (shorter wavelength, higher frequency). Nearly all distant galaxies show red shift, providing key evidence that the universe is expanding.
Doppler effect: motion causes wavelength shift
Red shift: wavelength increases (source moving away)
Blue shift: wavelength decreases (source moving towards)
Most galaxies show red shift: they're receding
Hubble's law: v = H₀d (velocity proportional to distance)
Cosmic microwave background: cooled radiation from early universe
Evidence points to Big Bang ~13.8 billion years ago
No centre to the expansion—it happens everywhere
Red shift is the increase in wavelength (decrease in frequency) of light observed from a source that is moving away from the observer.
— the entire absorption spectrum is shifted towards the red end (recall)
— using v = zc for v << c (calculation)

Hubble's law states that the recession velocity of a galaxy is directly proportional to its distance from us: v = H₀d, where H₀ ≈ 70 km/s per Mpc. This is significant because it shows the universe is expanding uniformly — the further away a galaxy is, the faster it recedes — implying everything was once much closer together.
— provides evidence for the Big Bang (recall + explanation)

If all distant galaxies show red shift, they are all moving away from us. Furthermore, more distant galaxies show greater red shift (receding faster). This is consistent with the expansion of space itself, rather than galaxies simply moving through space. The uniform expansion in all directions supports a universe that began in a concentrated state and has been expanding ever since.
— no preferred direction rules out a local explosion (explanation)

Imagine dots drawn on the surface of a balloon. As the balloon is inflated, every dot moves away from every other dot. No dot is at the centre of the expansion. Dots that are further apart separate faster. This demonstrates how galaxies recede from each other as space itself expands, with no centre to the expansion.

The CMB is low-level microwave radiation detected uniformly from all directions in space, corresponding to a temperature of about 2.7 K. It is the cooled remnant of the intense thermal radiation from the very hot, dense early universe (~380,000 years after the Big Bang). The radiation was originally high-energy but has been red shifted to microwaves by the expansion of space. Its existence was predicted by Big Bang theory before it was discovered.
By Hubble's law (v = H₀d), recession velocity is proportional to distance. Since Galaxy X is twice as far away as Galaxy Y, Galaxy X has twice the recession velocity of Galaxy Y.
